newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-News says settles Nine litigation.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-News says settles Nine litigation.

text.p: News Ltd managing director Lachlan Murdoch said on Thursday that litigation on all claims between the Nine Network Australia and News Ltd, The News Corp Ltd's Australian unit, had been settled on undisclosed terms.
The two companies were due in court later this year over a claim by Nine that News had breached an agreement to provide it with exclusive access to products from Twentieth Century Fox.

The dispute over the supply of Fox programming came while News Ltd's Super League was battling with the Australian Rugby League (ARL), backed by Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd chief Kerry Packer, for control of rugby league.

"This removes the final impediment between Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd and News Ltd in relation to Super League and allows us to concentrate on what we both do best," Murdoch said in a brief statement.
News and PBL also announced that Packer's Channel Nine had won the free-to-air broadcast rights for Monday night Super League matches.
Nine already holds the free-to-air rights for ARL matches.
"This deal does not in any way alter the Nine Network's existing contract with the ARL," PBL managing director James Packer said in a statement.
"We will continue to cover the ARL's competition on Friday nights and Saturday afternoons," Packer said.

"We also believe that the Nine Network telecasting both ARL and Super League will increase the prospect of a unified rugby league competition which, we believe, to be in the best interests of the public, viewers and all parties," Packer said.

Murdoch also welcomed the Super League with Channel Nine, saying Nine would also broadcast all matches from the Super League Tri-Series between New Zealand and Australian state sides New South Wales and Queensland.

Australia's three commercial free-to-air broadcasters had been invited to bid for Super League rights, with Murdoch adding that Channel Seven and Channel Ten could still bid for another weekly Super League match.
Super League matches will be shown on the pay-television network Foxtel, owned jointly by Rupert Murdoch's News Corp and Australian state telecommunications group Telstra.
Foxtel's rival Optus Vision own the pay-television rights to ARL matches. Optus was one of the ARL's major backers during the protracted and often bitter dispute with Super League.

Super League, an important part of Murdoch's global sports-driven pay-television network, won a major victory over the ARL last October when Australia's Federal Court ruled Murdoch's rugby league competition could begin next year.

Super League had appealed against an earlier ruling banning the rebel competition from starting before 2000. News Ltd invested A$270 million in its two-year battle with the ARL, the game's traditional rulers.
ARL chief executive Neil Whittaker told reporters he was disappointed by the deal between News Ltd and Channel Nine but said it did not signal a compromise between the two sides.
"Reading anymore into it is just fuelling speculation," Whittaker said.
"Of course we're disappointed but it's done. At least we now know whereabouts and when Super League will be on television," he said.
